text: Say you only want colors whose AVERAGE price is over 500 dollars. It's tempting to reach for WHERE. Let's see why that instinct fails, and what actually fixes it.

Where average of list price greater than 500 — this errors out. Remember from Lesson 11 that WHERE is evaluated BEFORE GROUP BY even runs. At that point in the process, groups don't exist yet, which means their averages don't exist yet either. WHERE filters individual rows. It has no concept of a group's aggregate result.

The fix is a clause built specifically for this: HAVING. Same query, HAVING average of list price greater than 500, placed AFTER group by instead of before it. This works because by the time HAVING runs, every group and its average already exist.

Let's put the real order together, because it's not the order you type things in. FROM comes first. Then WHERE, filtering individual rows. Then GROUP BY, forming the groups. Then HAVING, filtering those groups. Only after all of that does SELECT actually pick your columns, followed by ORDER BY at the very end.

And WHERE and HAVING aren't an either-or choice — use both together. Where color is not null removes rows with no color BEFORE grouping even starts. Then HAVING filters the resulting groups down to just the ones averaging over 500 dollars. Two different filters, for two different stages.
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after. Next lesson: UNION and UNION ALL, for stacking results from more than one query together. See you there.
